prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map separates a very near foreground basin/container and ledge (about 0.3–0.8 m from the camera) from the person, poles and work surface in front (roughly 1.5–3 m), with walls and upper scaffolding farther away (about 3–8 m). It makes the layered layout and relative distance of the large foreground object clearer than the RGB: it is within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach, while the main person is generally beyond reach and stands behind the crossing rails. Across the five frames, the main person stays at a broadly similar distance while moving from left-of-centre to the far right of view as the camera turns; foreground objects slide laterally and intermittently occlude the lower scene. Metric distances are uncertain because this is monocular depth, and the nearly white borders, dark openings, thin poles, reflective basin surfaces and frame edges show unreliable or smeared depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The map isolates several people in the first frame—including figures partly cut off at the far left—and one recurring person in later frames, making their locations and partial occlusions easier to distinguish from the dense scaffolding in the RGB. The recurring person is approximately 1.5–3 m in front of the camera, beyond the near foreground basin and rails, and shifts from left-of-centre through centre to the extreme right edge across time; the person generally faces toward the camera, although eye direction cannot be established. The people visible together in the first frame appear separated laterally by roughly 1–3 m, while parts of their bodies are hidden by image boundaries or scene structure; no person is clearly within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach. The segmentation is incomplete and unreliable for spatial inventory because most poles, containers, walls and foreground surfaces are unlabelled, some people disappear between frames, and the isolated “kite” label appears inconsistent with the RGB object.
descriptions.pose: The skeletons show the recurring person’s head, shoulders, torso and arms more distinctly than the RGB, placing the person upright about 1.5–3 m ahead and usually oriented roughly toward the camera wearer. Their hands remain close to their upper body rather than extending into the camera wearer’s space, so neither person appears mutually within arm’s reach; the map provides no skeleton for the camera wearer. Across frames two through five, the skeleton translates from left-of-centre to centre and then the far right edge, with modest changes in torso angle consistent with relative camera turning; the final skeleton is partly clipped by the right boundary. This map is unreliable for exact gaze, depth and limb placement: the first-frame people are missed, several joints are absent or clustered, lower legs are often not detected, and the final loose keypoints may be erroneous.
